mcqs.question: In a React Native FlatList, tapping a row updates selectedId in parent state, but the previously selected row never visually deselects. data did not change. Why?
options: FlatList is a PureComponent: values outside data that affect rendering must arrive through changed props, so pass extraData={selectedId}
The list needs getItemLayout so rows re-render at the new selection
keyExtractor must include the selection state so each row gets a fresh key
Each row must be wrapped in React.memo with default props
mcqs.explanation: Correct: FlatList is a PureComponent, so a re-render only happens when its props change; selection lives outside data, so it must be passed as extraData (React Native: https://reactnative.dev/docs/flatlist). The strongest distractor is option 3: baking selection into keys does force an update, but keys are identity, so every affected row remounts, losing row state and animations instead of updating in place.

mcqs.question: A team porting a web app to React Native assumes their existing DOM manipulation and CSS will keep working. Which statement reflects React Native's actual rendering model?
options: React components describe the UI, but core components map to native platform views, not browser DOM elements, so web CSS and browser APIs cannot be assumed to exist
The app renders inside a system web view, so existing DOM code keeps working after a small polyfill
React components are compiled to native source code at build time, so there is no JavaScript at runtime
The browser DOM is emulated on top of native views, so most web APIs work with minor differences
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the JavaScript side contains components and application logic while native projects bundle that JavaScript and render native components, so a web CSS or browser API must never be assumed (React Native: https://reactnative.dev/docs/components-and-apis). The strongest distractor is option 2: it describes a web-view approach, not React Native, whose core components map to real native views.

mcqs.question: After migrating to React Native's New Architecture, a team is surprised that startup time did not improve. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Serialization over the old bridge was probably not their bottleneck, and the app may need refactoring to benefit; the New Architecture enables capabilities rather than guaranteeing speedups
The migration was incomplete: JSI benefits require rewriting the components in C++
The old bridge is still running in parallel and must be deleted manually
Startup is always dominated by the bridge, so the measurement itself must be wrong
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the official guidance warns that an app may need refactoring and that serialization may not have been its bottleneck, so JSI-based interop and Fabric are capabilities, not automatic performance wins (React Native: https://reactnative.dev/architecture/landing-page). The strongest distractor is option 4: it denies the measurement instead of questioning the assumption, and it is exactly the belief that led the team to expect a guaranteed speedup.

mcqs.question: A team using Expo Go for daily development needs to integrate a third-party native library. What is the recommended move?
options: Move from Expo Go to a development build, which can include native libraries and production-like behavior
Eject to bare React Native immediately, because Expo cannot use native modules
Stay on Expo Go and mock the native library in development
Rebuild the app natively in Swift and Kotlin
mcqs.explanation: Correct: Expo Go is a limited playground, not the production development environment, so the move is a development build when native libraries or production-like behavior matter (Expo: https://docs.expo.dev/workflow/overview/). The strongest distractor is option 2: it is the classic eject myth; needing a native library is a limitation of the playground, not of the toolchain, and an Expo app is still a React Native app.

mcqs.question: What submission format does Google Play use for new app releases, and what does it do?
options: Android App Bundle: you upload the signed bundle and Play generates device-optimized APKs from it
A universal APK containing every density and architecture
An IPA package signed with the upload key
A signed release APK; App Bundles are optional and only for large teams
mcqs.explanation: Correct: Google Play uses Android App Bundles to generate device-optimized APKs, and requires signing (Google Play: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9859152). The strongest distractor is option 2: a universal APK is what internal testing builds produce, but shipping it to the store sends every device all code and assets and does not match Play's submission requirements.

scenarios.prompt: Users report two bugs in this list: (1) tapping a row updates selection on some rows but the previously selected row often stays highlighted, and (2) after a fast scroll, the list lands on the wrong message. Row bodies can wrap to two or three lines. Explain both bugs and fix the component.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Bug 1 is a PureComponent prop problem. FlatList is a PureComponent, so it only re-renders when its props change. Tapping a row changes selectedId in the parent, but data does not change, so from the list's perspective nothing it watches has changed and rows keep stale selection visuals. The fix is to pass the outside value as a changed prop: extraData={selectedId}. Do not fix it by baking selection into keyExtractor: keys are identity, and changing them remounts rows, destroying row state and animations. While here, also stabilize renderItem and row props: the inline closure and the inline onPress are recreated every render, which works against keeping unrelated state from redrawing cells; hoist renderItem or memoize it and pass a stable onPress callback. Bug 2 is a geometry contract violation. getItemLayout is only valid for fixed-size rows: it lets the list skip measurement by trusting the declared length and offset. Row bodies wrap to two or three lines, so real heights exceed 64, and every offset after a tall row is wrong; the list scrolls to computed positions that no longer match content, which shows up as landing on the wrong message. Either constrain rows to a true fixed height (for example, clamped or truncated bodies) or remove getItemLayout and let the list measure. Before tuning anything else, profile to confirm where the time actually goes, and validate the fix on a representative lower-end Android device rather than a simulator, because window sizes tuned on a simulator can blank content on real devices or waste memory.
rubric: Diagnoses bug 1 through FlatList being a PureComponent and fixes it with extraData, not key hacks
Diagnoses bug 2 as getItemLayout's fixed-geometry contract being violated by variable-height rows
Keeps renderItem and row props stable instead of recreating closures each render
Profiles before tuning knobs and adjusts windowing only against device measurements
Validates on a representative lower-end Android device, not only a simulator
